pr_reviewer_data.title: Add CI pipeline for Bun
pr_reviewer_data.description:
### Main Changes

This PR solve linting issues (c07419e) and introduce a new pipeline for running (`bun run validate`) against Bun versions from 1.0.0 to 1.3.0

### Assumptions
- I only included Ubuntu considering that most of Lodash requirements are related to JSC and not Bun API. So the CI take less to run and also the pipeline is cleaner.

### Context
- Related https://github.com/lodash/lodash/issues/6019
- The linting commit (c07419e) is also included in #6022 otherwise that PR will fail.

review_comments.body:
```suggestion
        run: npm i --lockfile-version 3 --package-lock-only
```
huh, `--frozen-lockfile` isn't a documented npm cli flag

I know this is from the `bun install` error message but Im wondering if they made a mistake, this is a yarn flag for sure though

Im guessing they wanted to  _only_ update the lockfile without installing anything, which is `--package-lock-only`. If they wanted `npm ci` type guard for not deviating from the lockfile, well `npm ci` and even `yarn --frozen-lockfile` wont write to the lockfile, so wouldnt do the version upgrade anyways.

pr_reviewer_data.title: security: Include a threat model
pr_reviewer_data.description:
### Main Changes

This PR include a new threat model (dadedacb12a74db6b572e95e69c5e442a3137759) and includes a new reference in the `SECURITY.md` (40bd77a63b253d82056ea9ee40a34ab4379c42ed)

Heavily inspired in Webpack ([ref](https://github.com/webpack/security-wg/blob/main/docs/threat-model.md)) and Express ([ref](https://github.com/expressjs/security-wg/blob/main/docs/ThreatModel.md)) threat models. This is an early version with the idea to help us during the security triage process.

**This PR is very open to feedback and suggestions.**

pr_reviewer_data.title: Fix make _.isNumber(NaN) return false and update tests
pr_reviewer_data.description:
### 📌 Fix: `_.isNumber(NaN)` now returns `false` as expected (Fixes #5981)

#### 🐛 The Issue
In Lodash v4.17.21, the `_.isNumber` function incorrectly returns `true` for `NaN`. This is problematic in scenarios where consumers of the library want to distinguish valid numbers from `NaN`.

**Reference:** [Issue #5981](https://github.com/lodash/lodash/issues/5981)

#### ✅ The Fix
The `isNumber` function has been updated to return `false` when the input is `NaN`. The logic now ensures that:
- Primitive `NaN` values are filtered out.
- Boxed `NaN` values (e.g., `Object(NaN)`) are also handled appropriately.

```js
    function isNumber(value) {
      return (typeof value == 'number' && !Number.isNaN(value)) ||  
             (isObjectLike(value) && baseGetTag(value) == numberTag);
    }
```

#### 🧪 Tests Updated
- Updated test case: `assert.strictEqual(_.isNumber(NaN), false);`
- Verified against full test suite using `pnpm test`.
- All tests passing ✅

pr_reviewer_data.title: Prevent prototype pollution chaining to code execution via _.template
pr_reviewer_data.description:
Prototype pollution is a common problem for Javascript applications.

[This paper (PDF-link)](https://github.com/HoLyVieR/prototype-pollution-nsec18/blob/master/paper/JavaScript_prototype_pollution_attack_in_NodeJS.pdf) is a reasonably comprehensive resource on the subject. It demonstrates that the problem is quite ubiquitous, and how it can turn into an unauthenticated RCE in Ghost, where the attack chain starts with a prototype pollution vulnerability in lodash.merge. Handlebars is used as the code execution gadget, but as Ghost also uses _.template it could have targeted that as well.

Lodash has had multiple prototype pollution vulnerabilities, [including recently](https://github.com/lodash/lodash/commit/1f8ea07746963a535385a5befc19fa687a627d2b).

If `_.template` is ever invoked after the prototype has been polluted, an attacker can execute any Javascript, as `sourceURL` and `variable` are looked up via an `options` object and injected into the Javascript that gets executed. If the caller is not passing those options (which is the most common usage), then the values from the potentially polluted prototype would be used instead. Here's the smallest possible POC:

```
// If the prototype is polluted via some other vulnerability
> ({}).__proto__.sourceURL = '\nconsole.log("injected code here")'
'\nconsole.log("injected code here")'
// ... then arbitrary code can be injected
> _.template('hey')({})
injected code here
'hey'
```

**I initially reached out via npm security**, and got the feedback that this is not considered an issue. (In the thread with NPM security I also provided examples of how to weaponise this against real applications instead of just the repl example. I can provide additional examples privately.)

I think it's worth fixing, as the fix is simple. Applications that are susceptible to prototype pollution will still need fixing, but at least the commonly used `_.template` shouldn't provide easy code execution.

(I've signed the CLA.)

pr_reviewer_data.title: Add optional resolveEmpty parameter to defaultTo
pr_reviewer_data.description:
This is an enhancement to Lodash that extends `defaultTo` with an optional `resolveEmpty` parameter. If supplied, `resolveEmpty` will be used to determine whether the passed `value` is empty and that `defaultValue` should be returned.

This would allow the following usage examples, amongst many others:

1. Default to a value when given a value considered empty by `lodash.isEmpty`:

```js
defaultTo('', defaultValue, isEmpty);
```

2. Default to a value after running `lodash.attempt` on a statement that may return an error using `lodash.isError`.

```js
defaultTo(attempt(require, filePath), defaultValue, isError);
```

[![CLA assistant check](https://cla.js.foundation/pull/badge/signed)](https://cla.js.foundation/lodash/lodash?pullRequest=4788)
All committers have signed the CLA.
I've seen this simplification in other code bases too. I'll think on it.

This simplification looks correct to me. (I was just looking at this code and thinking the same thing, and came here to see if there was already a PR for it.) It'd be good to have it merged, because it makes this function both more efficient and much simpler to understand.

Here's one way of thinking about why the existing code has the same behavior as the new code in this PR. The existing code says this:
```js
  if (Object.getPrototypeOf(value) === null) {
    return true
  }
  let proto = value		
  while (Object.getPrototypeOf(proto) !== null) {		
    proto = Object.getPrototypeOf(proto)		
  }		
  return Object.getPrototypeOf(value) === proto
```
The point is that the expression in that `return` at the end is asking precisely the question: did the loop body run exactly one time? And so the two `return` statements together are asking: would that loop run for either zero or one times?

Which is exactly what the new code says:
```js
  const proto = Object.getPrototypeOf(value)
  return proto === null || Object.getPrototypeOf(proto) === null
```

To see that the `return` at the end of the existing code is asking precisely whether the loop body ran exactly once, the main point is:
* On the one hand, after the loop body runs the first time, that condition `Object.getPrototypeOf(value) === proto` is true.
  * (It always runs at least once, because the first `return` means we don't get this far if it would run zero times.)
* If the condition `Object.getPrototypeOf(value) === proto` is ever true again, then that later value of `proto` is `===`-equal to the one we had after the first iteration.
  * That'd be a cycle in the prototype chain. I think that's forbidden by the spec.
  * But even if it can happen, it'd mean this is an infinite loop, and we'd never reach the final `return`.
* So if we get to the final `return` and the condition is true, we must have run the loop body exactly once.

---

That reasoning may look a little complicated. But all the complication is really from the existing code: the new code is much simpler and easier to understand. Merging this would mean that nobody else has to work through that reasoning again. :slightly_smiling_face:
